questions.question:
A ball is thrown vertically upwards at a speed of 2 m/s. What will be the maximum height attained and velocity of the body at the highest point, respectively, of the ball?

(Take g = 10 { m/s}² )
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**0.2 m and 0 m/s**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When an object is thrown **vertically upwards**, it moves against the force of gravity, which results in a constant deceleration.
 
• At the **highest point** of its trajectory, the object momentarily stops before it begins its descent. Therefore, the **final velocity (v)** at the maximum height is always **0 m/s**.
 
• To find the **maximum height (H)**, we use the third equation of motion: **v² = u² + 2as**, where **v** is final velocity, **u** is initial velocity, **a** is acceleration, and **s** is displacement (height).
 
• Given data: Initial velocity **(u) = 2 m/s**, Final velocity **(v) = 0 m/s**, and acceleration due to gravity **(g) = 10 m/s²**. Since the motion is upwards, acceleration **(a) = -g = -10 m/s²**.
 
• Calculation: **(0)² = (2)² + 2(-10)H**. This simplifies to **0 = 4 - 20H**. Solving for H, we get **20H = 4**, which results in **H = 4/20 = 0.2 m**.
 
• Thus, the **maximum height attained is 0.2 m** and the **velocity at the highest point is 0 m/s**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Equations of Motion**: These equations describe the relationship between **velocity, distance, time, and acceleration** for objects moving with uniform acceleration. The three primary equations are **v = u + at**, **s = ut + ½at²**, and **v² = u² + 2as**.
 
• **Acceleration due to Gravity (g)**: This is the acceleration gained by an object due to the **gravitational force** of the Earth. Its value is approximately **9.8 m/s²** near the Earth's surface, but for competitive exams, it is often approximated as **10 m/s²**.
 
• **Time of Ascent**: This is the time taken by an object to reach its maximum height. Using the formula **v = u + at**, where **0 = 2 - 10t**, the time of ascent for this ball is **0.2 seconds**.
 
• **Kinematics of Vertical Motion**: In a vacuum (ignoring air resistance), the **Time of Ascent** is always equal to the **Time of Descent**. The speed at which the ball is thrown up will be equal to the speed at which it returns to the starting point.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Sign Convention**: It is crucial to assign signs correctly. Usually, **upward direction** is taken as positive and **downward direction** as negative. Since gravity always pulls **downward**, **g** is taken as **-10 m/s²** when the object is moving up.
 
• **Zero Velocity at Peak**: A common misconception is that acceleration is zero at the peak. However, while **velocity is 0 m/s** at the highest point, **acceleration** remains constant at **10 m/s²** downwards throughout the entire flight.
 
• **Displacement vs. Distance**: If the ball returns to the thrower's hand, the **total displacement is 0 m**, while the **total distance** covered would be **0.4 m** (0.2 m up + 0.2 m down).
 
• **Independence of Mass**: In the absence of air resistance, the **maximum height** attained by an object depends only on its **initial velocity** and gravity, not on the **mass** of the ball.

questions.question: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance of the combination is:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1 Ω**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When resistors are connected in a **parallel combination**, the reciprocal of the **equivalent resistance (Rp)** is equal to the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances.
 
• The mathematical formula for three resistors in parallel is **1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3**. In this case, the values are **2 Ω**, **3 Ω**, and **6 Ω**.
 
• Applying the values: **1/Rp = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6**. To solve this, we find a common denominator, which is **6**. The calculation becomes **3/6 + 2/6 + 1/6 = 6/6**.
 
• Solving for **Rp**, we get **1/Rp = 1**, which means the **equivalent resistance** is **1 Ω**. ***Hence, the correct answer is 1 Ω.***
 
• A fundamental characteristic of **parallel circuits** is that the **total resistance** is always less than the value of the **smallest individual resistor** in the combination. Since **1 Ω** is less than **2 Ω**, the result is consistent with physical laws.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Series Combination:**

 
 
• In a **series circuit**, the total resistance is the algebraic sum of individual resistances: **Rs = R1 + R2 + R3**.
 
• If these three resistors (**2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω**) were connected in series, the equivalent resistance would be **11 Ω**.
 
• In series, the **current** remains constant through all components, but the **voltage** drops across each resistor.
 
 
 
• **Domestic Wiring Systems:**
 
 
• Most **household electrical appliances** are connected in **parallel**.
 
• This arrangement ensures that every appliance receives the same **voltage (220V in India)** and can be operated independently using separate switches.
 
• If one appliance fails or is turned off in a **parallel circuit**, the others continue to function normally.
 
 
 
• **Ohm's Law:**
 
 
• Formulated by **Georg Simon Ohm** in **1827**, it states that the current (I) through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference (V) across it, provided physical conditions remain constant: **V = IR**.
 
• The **SI unit** of resistance is the **Ohm**, symbolized by the Greek letter **Ω (Omega)**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Factors Affecting Resistance:** The resistance of a conductor depends on its **length** (directly proportional), **area of cross-section** (inversely proportional), the **nature of the material** (resistivity), and **temperature**.
 
• **Conductance:** The reciprocal of resistance is called **conductance (G)**, measured in **Siemens (S)** or **mho**. In parallel circuits, the total conductance is simply the sum of individual conductances (**Gp = G1 + G2 + G3**).
 
• **Current Distribution:** In a **parallel combination**, the total current from the source is divided among the branches. The branch with the **lowest resistance** (the **2 Ω** resistor in this example) will carry the **highest current**.
 
• **Power Dissipation:** In parallel, the resistor with the **lowest resistance** dissipates the **most power** since Power **P = V² / R** and V is constant for all.

questions.question: If the frequency of a vibrating object is 50 { Hz} , what is its time period?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**0.02 s**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **frequency** of a vibrating object is defined as the total number of oscillations or vibrations it completes in **one second**.
 
• The **time period** (T) is the duration required to complete **one single vibration** or cycle.
 
• There is a fundamental mathematical relationship between these two properties: they are the **reciprocal** of each other. The formula is expressed as **T = 1 / f**, where **f** represents the **frequency**.
 
• Given the data in the question, the **frequency** (f) is **50 Hz**. To find the **time period**, we apply the formula: **T = 1 / 50**.
 
• By performing the division, **1 divided by 50** equals **0.02**. Therefore, the **time period** of the vibrating object is **0.02 s**. ***Hence, the correct answer is 0.02 s.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Frequency and Units:**

 
 
• The **SI unit** of **frequency** is the **Hertz**, abbreviated as **Hz**. It is named after the famous **19th-century** German physicist **Heinrich Rudolf Hertz**, who proved the existence of electromagnetic waves.
 
• A frequency of **1 Hz** means that **one vibration** occurs every **one second**. In this context, **50 Hz** implies that the object is vibrating **50 times** every **one second**.
 
 
 
• **Time Period Characteristics:**
 
 
• The **SI unit** for the **time period** is the **second (s)**.
 
• In wave mechanics, the **time period** remains constant for a stable source, even if the wave travels through different media, provided the source **frequency** does not change.
 
 
 
• **Physical Examples:**
 
 
• **Sound Waves**: The **frequency** of a sound wave determines its **pitch**. A high-frequency vibration produces a **high-pitched** sound (like a whistle), while a low-frequency vibration produces a **low-pitched** sound (like a bass drum).
 
• **Power Supply**: In **India**, the standard **frequency** of the **Alternating Current (AC)** supplied to homes is **50 Hz**, which matches the value provided in this problem.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Inverse Proportion**: The **frequency** and the **time period** are in **inverse proportion**. If the **frequency** of an object doubles, its **time period** is halved.
 
• **Calculation Tip**: To quickly calculate **1/50**, one can multiply both the numerator and the denominator by **2**, resulting in **2/100**, which clearly equals **0.02**.
 
• **Vibratory Motion**: This type of motion is characterized by a "to-and-fro" movement about a central **mean position**. Common examples include the movement of a **simple pendulum**, the prongs of a **tuning fork**, or the strings of a **guitar**.
 
• **Audible Range**: For humans, the audible **frequency** range is typically between **20 Hz** and **20,000 Hz**. Any vibration with a **frequency** below **20 Hz** is called **infrasonic**, and above **20,000 Hz** is called **ultrasonic**.

questions.question: A sound of 100 { Hz} is compared with a sound of 500 { Hz} . Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: 100 Hz sound has a higher pitch.
500 Hz sound has a higher pitch.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**500 Hz sound has a higher pitch**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pitch** is a sensory characteristic of sound that allows a listener to assign it a position on a musical scale based on its **frequency**. It determines how "shrill" or "grave" a sound appears to the human ear.
 
• The **frequency** of a sound wave is defined as the number of **vibrations** or cycles completed per unit of time, specifically per **second**. The standard unit for measuring frequency is **Hertz (Hz)**.
 
• There is a direct proportional relationship between frequency and pitch: a sound with a **higher frequency** will always have a **higher pitch**, while a sound with a **lower frequency** will have a **lower pitch**.
 
• In the given comparison, the sound of **500 Hz** completes **500 cycles per second**, whereas the sound of **100 Hz** completes only **100 cycles per second**. Therefore, the **500 Hz** sound is much more shrill. ***Hence, the statement "500 Hz sound has a higher pitch" is correct.***
 
• The statement that both have the same pitch is false because pitch is strictly dependent on frequency, and these two frequencies are different. ***Hence, the statement "Both have the same pitch" is incorrect.***
 
• The statement claiming the 100 Hz sound is higher is physically impossible under standard acoustic laws because **100 Hz** is a lower frequency than **500 Hz**. ***Hence, the statement "100 Hz sound has a higher pitch" is incorrect.***
 
• Since pitch is a measurable and quantifiable property related to frequency, it can easily be compared using objective data. ***Hence, the statement "Pitch cannot be compared" is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Human Audibility Range**: The standard range of **audible frequencies** for a healthy human ear is between **20 Hz** and **20,000 Hz** (or **20 kHz**). Frequency values outside this range are generally not perceived as sound by humans.
 
• **Infrasonic and Ultrasonic**: Sounds with a frequency lower than **20 Hz** are categorized as **infrasonic** (e.g., sounds produced by elephants or earthquakes). Sounds with a frequency higher than **20,000 Hz** are **ultrasonic** (e.g., sounds used by bats for navigation or in medical **ultrasound** imaging).
 
• **Loudness vs. Pitch**: It is crucial to distinguish pitch from **loudness**. **Pitch** depends on **frequency**, whereas **loudness** depends on the **amplitude** (the maximum displacement of the particles of the medium). A sound can be high-pitched but very quiet, or low-pitched and very loud.
 
• **Wavelength Relationship**: Frequency and **wavelength** are inversely proportional. This means a high-pitched **500 Hz** sound has a **shorter wavelength**, while a low-pitched **100 Hz** sound has a **longer wavelength**, assuming they travel through the same medium like **air** at a constant **temperature**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Biological Factors**: In humans, the pitch of the voice is determined by the **vocal cords**. **Women** and **children** typically have shorter and thinner vocal cords that vibrate faster, producing a **higher frequency** and thus a **higher pitch** voice compared to adult **men**.
 
• **Speed of Sound**: The **speed of sound** in a specific medium (such as dry air at **20 degrees Celsius**, where it is approximately **343 meters per second**) is independent of the frequency. Therefore, both the **100 Hz** and **500 Hz** sounds travel at the **same speed** in the same environment.
 
• **Musical Octaves**: In music, an **octave** is the interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency. For example, a note at **500 Hz** is approximately one octave higher than a note at **250 Hz**.

questions.question: When a current of 1 A flows through an electric geyser for 10 seconds, 100 J of heat is generated. What is the resistance of the geyser?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**10 Ω**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The amount of heat produced in a conductor when an electric current passes through it is governed by **Joule’s Law of Heating**. According to this law, the heat generated (**H**) is directly proportional to the square of the **current** (**I**), the **resistance** (**R**) of the conductor, and the **time** (**t**) for which the current flows.
 
• The mathematical expression for this law is **H = I²Rt**. In this equation, **H** is measured in **Joules** (**J**), **I** in **Amperes** (**A**), **R** in **Ohms** (**Ω**), and **t** in **seconds** (**s**).
 
• In the given problem, the current (**I**) is **1 A**, the time (**t**) is **10 seconds**, and the heat produced (**H**) is **100 J**.
 
• To find the resistance, we rearrange the formula to **R = H / (I²t)**. Substituting the known values: **R = 100 / (1² × 10)**.
 
• This simplifies to **R = 100 / 10**, which equals **10 Ω**. ***Hence, the resistance of the geyser is 10 Ω, making option 1 the correct answer.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Electric Geyser:** It is an appliance that converts **electrical energy** into **heat energy**. It uses a **heating element** made of materials with **high resistance** and **high melting point**, such as **Nichrome** (an alloy of nickel and chromium).
 
• **Resistance (R):** It is the property of a conductor to oppose the flow of **electric current**. The **SI unit** of resistance is the **Ohm**, named after the German physicist **Georg Simon Ohm**. Resistance depends on the **length**, **area of cross-section**, **nature of the material**, and **temperature**.
 
• **Current (I):** It is defined as the **rate of flow of electric charge** through a cross-section of a conductor. Its **SI unit** is the **Ampere** (**A**), and it is measured using an instrument called an **ammeter**.
 
• **Electrical Energy and Power:** Power (**P**) is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed, given by **P = VI** or **P = I²R**. Heat (**H**) is simply the power multiplied by time (**H = P × t**).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Joule's Law Discovery:** The heating effect of current was studied experimentally by **James Prescott Joule** in the year **1841**. It is a fundamental principle used in domestic appliances like **electric irons**, **toasters**, **ovens**, and **heaters**.
 
• **Units Consistency:** When solving numerical problems related to **Joule's Law**, it is crucial to ensure that **time** is always in **seconds**. If time is given in minutes or hours, it must be converted (**1 minute = 60 seconds**).
 
• **Practical Application:** In a **geyser**, the resistance is designed such that for a standard **voltage** (usually **220V** in India), the current flowing through it produces enough heat to raise the water temperature efficiently within a reasonable **time**.
 
• **Safety Feature:** Most heating appliances include a **thermostat** to break the circuit once a certain temperature is reached, preventing damage due to excessive heat production.

questions.question: A car starts from rest and reaches a speed of 72 km/hr in 20 seconds. What is the acceleration of the car?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1 m/s²**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Acceleration is defined as the **rate of change of velocity**.
 
• The formula for acceleration is: **a = (v − u)/t**
 
• Given:
 
 
• Initial velocity, **u = 0 m/s** (car starts from rest)
 
• Final velocity, **v = 72 km/h = 20 m/s** (since 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s)
 
• Time, **t = 20 s**
 
 
 
• Substituting the values:

 **a = (20 − 0)/20 = 1 m/s²**
 
• ***Hence, the acceleration of the car is 1 m/s².***

• Metre per second squared (**m/s²**).

• **1 km/h = 5/18 m/s**.
 
• To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by **5/18**.
 
 
 
• **Types of Motion:**
 
 
• If acceleration is constant, the motion is called **uniformly accelerated motion**.

questions.question: If a particle covers a distance of 12 m in every 3 s, what is the slope of its distance-time graph?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**4.0 m/s**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **slope** of a **distance-time graph** is a physical representation of the **speed** of an object. In physics, the slope is defined as the vertical change (rise) divided by the horizontal change (run).
 
• In this specific problem, the particle covers a **distance** of **12 m** in every **3 s**. This indicates that the particle is moving at a **constant rate**, which is a characteristic of **uniform motion**.
 
• To calculate the **slope**, we use the formula: **Slope = Change in Distance / Change in Time**. This is equivalent to the formula for speed: **v = d / t**.
 
• By substituting the given numerical values into the formula: **Slope = 12 m / 3 s**. Performing the division gives a result of **4.0 m/s**.
 
• Since the **slope** is **4.0 m/s**, it tells us that for every **1 second** that passes, the particle moves exactly **4 meters**. The **linear** nature of the graph (a straight line) confirms that the **speed** remains **constant** throughout the motion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Distance-Time Graph Fundamentals:**

 
 
• On a **distance-time graph**, the **time** is always plotted on the **x-axis** (the independent variable), and the **distance** is plotted on the **y-axis** (the dependent variable).
 
• The **unit** for the slope in this graph is **meters per second (m/s)**, which is the standard **SI unit** for **speed**.
 
 
 
• **Types of Motion on Graphs:**
 
 
• **Uniform Motion:** Represented by a **straight line** passing through the origin. The **constant slope** indicates a **constant speed**.
 
• **Non-Uniform Motion:** Represented by a **curved line** (parabola). A curve indicates that the object is **accelerating** or **decelerating**, meaning the **speed** is changing over time.
 
• **Object at Rest:** Represented by a **horizontal line** parallel to the time axis. In this case, the **slope** is **0**, indicating a **speed** of **0 m/s**.
 
 
 
• **Speed vs. Velocity:**
 
 
• While the slope of a **distance-time graph** gives the **speed** (a **scalar quantity**), the slope of a **displacement-time graph** provides the **velocity** (a **vector quantity**).
 
• Speed only considers **magnitude**, whereas velocity considers both **magnitude** and **direction**.
 
 
 
• **Graphical Interpretation:**
 
 
• A **steeper line** on the graph indicates a **higher slope** and thus a **greater speed**. Conversely, a line with a **low angle** of inclination indicates a **slower speed**.
 
• If the line is **vertical**, it would imply **infinite speed** (covering distance in zero time), which is physically impossible for a particle with mass.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The calculation of the slope **12 / 3 = 4** is a direct application of the **rate of change** concept in **kinematics**.
 
• In **calculus** terms, the **speed** is the **first derivative** of **distance** with respect to **time** (**v = dd/dt**). For **linear graphs**, this derivative is simply the **constant slope** of the line.
 
• Understanding **distance-time graphs** is crucial for analyzing **real-world data**, such as the **average speed** of vehicles, **satellite orbits**, or **athletic performance**.

questions.question: What is the mass number of a neutral atom with 11 electrons, 11 protons and 12 neutrons?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**23**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **mass number** of an atom is the sum of the number of protons and neutrons in its nucleus. The formula is:

 **Mass Number = Number of Protons + Number of Neutrons**.
 
• In the given case, the atom has **11 protons** and **12 neutrons**. Thus, the mass number can be calculated as: **Mass Number = 11 + 12 = 23**.
 
• The atom is described as **neutral**. This means the number of protons (positively charged) equals the number of electrons (negatively charged). Hence, the atom has **11 electrons** as it has 11 protons.
 
• The **mass number** does not include electrons since their mass is negligible compared to protons and neutrons.
 
• Therefore, the correct mass number of this neutral atom is **23**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Atomic Number:**

 
 
• The **atomic number** is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. It defines the chemical element. For example, an atom with **11 protons** has an atomic number of **11**, which corresponds to the element **sodium (Na)**.
 
• The number of electrons in a neutral atom equals its atomic number. In this case, the atom has **11 electrons**.
 
 
 
• **Isotopes:**
 
 
• Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons, leading to different **mass numbers**. These are called **isotopes**.
 
• For instance, the isotopes of hydrogen include **protium (1 proton, 0 neutrons, mass number = 1)**, **deuterium (1 proton, 1 neutron, mass number = 2)**, and **tritium (1 proton, 2 neutrons, mass number = 3)**.
 
 
 
• **Subatomic Particles:**
 
 
• Atoms are composed of three main subatomic particles: **Protons** (positively charged, located in the nucleus), **Neutrons** (neutral, located in the nucleus), and **Electrons** (negatively charged, orbiting the nucleus).
 
• Protons and neutrons have approximately the same mass, which is significantly larger than the mass of electrons. Hence, they contribute most to the atom's mass.
 
 
 
• **Mass Number vs Atomic Mass:**
 
 
• The **mass number** is a whole number representing the total number of protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus.
 
• The **atomic mass** is a weighted average of all the isotopes of an element, expressed in atomic mass units (amu).
 
• For example, the atomic mass of sodium is approximately **22.99 amu**, while its most common isotope has a mass number of **23**.

questions.question: A resistor of 4 Omega produces 64 J of heat every second. What is the potential difference across it?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**16 V**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The problem involves calculating the **potential difference (V)** across a resistor using the given data of heat produced and resistance.
 
• The relationship between heat, current, and resistance is derived from the formula for power dissipation: **P = I²R**, where P is power, I is current, and R is resistance.
 
• Given that the resistor produces **64 J of heat every second**, this indicates that the **power (P)** is 64 W (since power is energy per unit time).
 
• To find the current (I), use the formula: **P = I²R**. Rearranging gives: **I = √(P/R)**. Substituting the values:

 I = √(64/4) = √16 = 4 A.
 
• Next, use Ohm’s Law: **V = IR**, to calculate the potential difference. Substituting the values:

 V = 4 × 4 = 16 V.
 
• **Hence, the correct answer is 16 V.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ohm’s Law:**

 
 
• Ohm's Law states that the current (I) through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage (V) across the two points and inversely proportional to the resistance (R).
 
• The mathematical expression is: **V = IR**.
 
• This law is fundamental in circuit analysis and is used to calculate voltage, current, or resistance in electrical circuits.
 
 
 
• **Power in Electrical Circuits:**
 
 
• Electrical power is the rate at which electrical energy is transferred by an electric circuit. It is measured in **watts (W)**.
 
• The formula for power is: **P = V × I**, where P is power, V is voltage, and I is current.
 
• Alternatively, using Ohm's Law, power can also be expressed as: **P = I²R** or **P = V²/R**.
 
 
 
• **Resistance:**
 
 
• Resistance is a measure of the opposition to the flow of electric current in a circuit. It is measured in **ohms (Ω)**.
 
• Factors affecting resistance include the material, length, and cross-sectional area of the conductor, as well as temperature.
 
• Resistors are components specifically designed to provide a certain amount of resistance in electrical circuits.
 
 
 
• **Heat Produced by a Resistor:**
 
 
• When current flows through a resistor, electrical energy is converted into heat energy. This phenomenon is described by **Joule’s Law of Heating**.
 
• The heat produced is directly proportional to the square of the current, the resistance, and the time for which the current flows: **H = I²Rt**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Unit of Power:** The unit of power is **watt (W)**, where 1 watt equals 1 joule per second.
 
• **Unit of Resistance:** The unit of resistance is **ohm (Ω)**, named after the German physicist **Georg Simon Ohm**.
 
• **Practical Applications:** Understanding these concepts is essential for designing electrical appliances, power systems, and electronic devices.
 
• **Safety Note:** Excessive heat generated by resistors can damage circuits, so proper heat dissipation mechanisms, such as heat sinks or fans, are often employed.

questions.question: The refractive indices of water, glass and diamond are 1.33, 1.5, and 2.42, respectively. Light travels:

options.text: at the same speed irrespective of the medium

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**the fastest in water medium**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **refractive index** (represented as **n**) of a medium is defined as the ratio of the **speed of light in a vacuum** (c) to the **speed of light in that specific medium** (v). The formula is expressed as **n = c / v**.
 
• Based on this formula, the velocity of light in a medium is **inversely proportional** to its refractive index. This means light travels **faster** in a medium with a **lower refractive index** and **slower** in a medium with a **higher refractive index**.
 
• Comparing the given values: the refractive index of **water is 1.33**, **glass is 1.5**, and **diamond is 2.42**.
 
• Since **water** has the **lowest refractive index** (**1.33**) among the three, light encounters the least optical resistance, and therefore, **light travels the fastest in water**. ***Hence, option 1 is correct.***
 
• Light does not travel at the same speed in different media because each medium has a different **optical density**. ***Hence, option 2 is incorrect.***
 
• In **glass**, light travels slower than in water because **1.5 is greater than 1.33**. ***Hence, option 3 is incorrect.***
 
• In **diamond**, light travels the **slowest** because it has the **highest refractive index** (**2.42**) provided in the list. ***Hence, option 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Optical Density:** A medium with a higher refractive index is said to be **optically denser**, while a medium with a lower refractive index is **optically rarer**. Light waves are delayed by interactions with the atoms in a denser medium.
 
• **Speed of Light in Vacuum:** The speed of light in a vacuum is a universal physical constant, approximately **299,792,458 meters per second** (often simplified to **3 x 10⁸ m/s**).
 
• **Refraction Phenomenon:** When light moves from an **optically rarer medium** (like water) to an **optically denser medium** (like glass), it **bends towards the normal** and its speed decreases. Conversely, it bends away from the normal when entering a rarer medium.
 
• **Diamond's Brilliance:** The high refractive index of **diamond** (**2.42**) is responsible for its extraordinary sparkle. It causes **Total Internal Reflection (TIR)** of light within the gemstone, trapping the light and reflecting it multiple times before it exits.
 
• **Unitless Quantity:** The refractive index is a **dimensionless number** because it is a ratio of two similar quantities (speeds).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Velocity Calculations:** By using the constant speed of light **c = 3 x 10⁸ m/s**, we can calculate the approximate speeds in these media:

 
 
• Speed in **Water**: 3 x 10⁸ / 1.33 ≈ **2.25 x 10⁸ m/s**.
 
• Speed in **Glass**: 3 x 10⁸ / 1.5 = **2.0 x 10⁸ m/s**.
 
• Speed in **Diamond**: 3 x 10⁸ / 2.42 ≈ **1.24 x 10⁸ m/s**.
 
 
 
• **Medium Dependency:** The refractive index of a material can also vary slightly depending on the **wavelength** of the light (color) and the **temperature** of the medium.
 
• **Historical Context:** The concept of refractive index is fundamental to **Snell's Law**, which describes the relationship between the angles of incidence and refraction for light passing through a boundary between two different isotropic media.

questions.question: A convex lens has a focal length of 25 cm. What is the power of this convex lens?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**+4.0 D**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

• The **power of a lens** is the ability of the lens to converge or diverge light rays passing through it. It is measured in **dioptres (D)**.
 
• The formula to calculate the power of a lens is:

 **P = 100 / f**, where **P** is the power in dioptres and **f** is the focal length in centimeters.
 
• In the given question, the focal length of the convex lens is **25 cm**. Substituting this into the formula:

 **P = 100 / 25 = +4.0 D**.
 
• A **positive power (+)** indicates that the lens is a **convex lens**, which converges light rays.
 
• Hence, the power of the convex lens is **+4.0 D**, and **this is the correct answer.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Convex Lens:**

 
 
• A convex lens is also known as a **converging lens** because it brings parallel rays of light to a focus.
 
• It is thicker at the center and thinner at the edges.
 
• Convex lenses are commonly used in devices like **magnifying glasses, cameras, and projectors**.
 
 
 
• **Dioptre:**
 
 
• The dioptre (D) is the unit of measurement for the optical power of a lens or a curved mirror.
 
• It is defined as the reciprocal of the focal length in meters (**D = 1/f**), where **f** is in meters.
 
• A positive dioptre value indicates a converging lens (convex), while a negative value indicates a diverging lens (concave).
 
 
 
• **Lens Power and Focal Length:**
 
 
• The focal length (**f**) of a lens is the distance from the center of the lens to the point where light rays converge or diverge.
 
• The shorter the focal length, the higher the optical power of the lens.
 
• For example, a lens with a focal length of 50 cm has a power of **+2.0 D**, while a lens with a focal length of 25 cm has a power of **+4.0 D**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Convex Lenses:**
 
 
• Convex lenses are used in **eyeglasses** to correct farsightedness (hyperopia).
 
• They are also used in **microscopes** and **telescopes** for magnification purposes.
 
• Other applications include their use in **optical instruments**, cameras, and focusing systems.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Power of Concave Lens:**

 
 
• A concave lens is a **diverging lens**, and its power is represented by a **negative** value.
 
• For example, if the focal length of a concave lens is 50 cm, its power is **-2.0 D**.
 
 
 
• **Difference Between Convex and Concave Lenses:**
 
 
• **Convex Lens:** Converges light rays, has positive power, and is thicker at the center.
 
• **Concave Lens:** Diverges light rays, has negative power, and is thinner at the center.
 
 
 
• **Real and Virtual Images:**
 
 
• A convex lens can form both **real and virtual images**, depending on the position of the object.
 
• A concave lens, however, always forms a **virtual image**.

__
 
• **Work done (W)** is calculated using the formula: **W = F × d × cos(θ)**, where:

 
 
• **F** is the force applied (10 N).
 
• **d** is the displacement of the object (5 m).
 
• **θ** is the angle between the force and displacement direction (**0°** since the force is applied in the direction of movement).
 
 
 
• Substituting the values into the formula:
 
 
• W = 10 × 5 × cos(0°).
 
• Since cos(0°) = 1, the equation becomes W = 10 × 5 × 1 = **50 J**.
 
 
 
• The **work done** is measured in **joules (J)**, which is the SI unit of work and energy.
 
• Since the force is applied in the same direction as the displacement, the full magnitude of the force contributes to the work done.
 
• **Hence, the correct answer is 50 J.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• Work is defined as the energy transferred to or from an object via the application of force along a displacement.
 
• It is mathematically expressed as **W = F × d × cos(θ)**, where:
 
 
• **F** = magnitude of the force.
 
• **d** = displacement of the object.
 
• **θ** = angle between the force and displacement vectors.
 
 
 
• Work is **positive** when the force and displacement are in the same direction and **negative** when they are in opposite directions.
 
 
 
• **Energy and Work:**
 
 
• Work is closely related to energy. When work is done on an object, energy is transferred to or from that object.
 
• The unit of both work and energy in the **SI system** is the **joule (J)**.
 
• 1 joule is defined as the work done when a force of 1 newton moves an object 1 meter in the direction of the force.
 
 
 
• **Force:**
 
 
• Force is defined as an interaction that, when unopposed, changes the motion of an object.
 
• The SI unit of force is the **newton (N)**, and 1 newton is equivalent to 1 kg·m/s².
 
• In this problem, a force of **10 N** is applied to the object.
 
 
 
• **Displacement:**
 
 
• Displacement is a vector quantity that refers to the change in position of an object.
 
• In this problem, the object is displaced by **5 m** in the direction of the applied force.
 
 
 
• **Angle between Force and Displacement:**
 
 
• The angle between the force and displacement is crucial in calculating work.
 
• When θ = 0°, cos(θ) = 1, and the entire force contributes to the work.
 
• If θ = 90°, cos(θ) = 0, and no work is done.

• The object must be displaced due to the force.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The problem can be solved using the **equations of motion** under **constant acceleration**. Since the ball is dropped from rest, the **initial velocity (u)** is **0 m/s**.
 
• The ball falls through a **vertical distance (s)** of **20 meters**. This represents the **displacement** of the object.
 
• The **acceleration (a)** acting on the ball is the **acceleration due to gravity (g)**, which is given as **10 m/s²**. *Hence, the values for u, s, and g are established.*
 
• The **third equation of motion** relates velocity, acceleration, and distance: **v² = u² + 2as**. Plugging in the known values, we get **v² = 0² + 2(10)(20)**.
 
• Calculating the product, **v² = 400**. Taking the **square root** of **400**, we find the **final velocity (v)** to be **20.0 m/s**. *Hence, the calculated velocity is 20.0 m/s.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Equations of Motion:**

 
 
• These equations were formulated by **Sir Isaac Newton** and describe the relationship between **velocity**, **time**, **acceleration**, and **displacement** for an object moving with **uniform acceleration**.
 
• The three primary equations are: **v = u + at**, **s = ut + 1/2 at²**, and **v² = u² + 2as**.
 
• In this context, **v** is the **final velocity**, **u** is the **initial velocity**, **a** is the **acceleration**, **t** is the **time**, and **s** is the **displacement**.
 
 
 
• **Acceleration due to Gravity:**
 
 
• On **Earth**, the average value of **g** is approximately **9.8 m/s²**, but for simplicity in competitive exams and school calculations, it is often taken as **10 m/s²**.
 
• The value of **g** varies slightly depending on the **location** (latitude and altitude) on the Earth's surface.
 
• This acceleration is always directed **downwards** towards the **center of the Earth**.
 
 
 
• **Free Fall Concept:**
 
 
• A **free-falling object** is an object that is falling under the **sole influence of gravity**.
 
• In a **vacuum**, all objects fall at the **same rate** regardless of their **mass**, as demonstrated by **Galileo Galilei**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Sign Convention:** While solving physics problems, defining a **direction** as positive is crucial. If **downward motion** is considered positive, then both **acceleration (g)** and **displacement (s)** will be **positive**.
 
• **Mass Independence:** Note that the **mass** of the ball was not provided and is **not required** to calculate the final velocity in a free fall scenario, assuming **air resistance** is negligible.

questions.question: A body of mass 5 { kg} is moving with an acceleration of 2 { m/s}² . What is the force acting on it?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**10 N**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to **Newton's Second Law of Motion**, the **force** acting on an object is directly proportional to the product of its **mass** and **acceleration**. This fundamental principle of **Classical Mechanics** provides the quantitative description of force.
 
• The mathematical expression for this law is **F = m x a**, where **F** is the **net force**, **m** is the **mass** of the body, and **a** is the **acceleration** produced.
 
• In the provided problem, the **mass (m)** of the body is given as **5 kg** and the **acceleration (a)** is **2 m/s2**.
 
• By applying the formula, the **Force (F)** is calculated as **5 kg multiplied by 2 m/s2**, which equals **10 kg.m/s2** or **10 N**. ***Hence, the statement regarding the force being 10 N is correct.***
 
• The unit of **force** in the **International System of Units (SI)** is the **Newton**, symbolized by **N**. One **Newton** is defined as the **amount of force** required to provide an **acceleration** of **1 m/s2** to a **mass** of **1 kg**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Newton's Laws of Motion:**

 
 
• **Sir Isaac Newton** first presented these **three laws** in his work **Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica**, published in the **year 1687**.
 
• **First Law (Law of Inertia):** An object will remain at **rest** or move in a **straight line** at a **constant velocity** unless acted upon by an **external force**.
 
• **Third Law (Action and Reaction):** For every **action force**, there is an **equal and opposite reaction force** acting on two different bodies.
 
 
 
• **Vector Nature of Force:**
 
 
• **Force** is a **vector quantity**, meaning it possesses both **magnitude** and **direction**.
 
• In this calculation, the **magnitude** is **10 N**, and the **direction** of the force would be the same as the **direction** of the **acceleration**.
 
 
 
• **Mass vs. Weight:**
 
 
• The **mass** of an object (measured in **kg**) is a measure of its **inertia** and remains **constant** regardless of **location**.
 
• The **weight** is the **gravitational force** acting on that **mass**, calculated as **W = m x g**, where **g** is approximately **9.8 m/s2** on **Earth**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **SI Unit Conversion:** The **Newton (N)** can be broken down into **base units** as **kg.m.s-2**. In the **CGS system**, the unit of **force** is the **dyne**, where **1 Newton** is equal to **100,000 (10⁵) dynes**.
 
• **Concept of Net Force:** The **Newton's Second Law** specifically refers to the **net force** (the **vector sum** of all **individual forces**) acting on the body. If multiple **forces** act in **opposite directions**, they must be **subtracted** to find the **resultant force**.
 
• **Applications:** This principle is used in **engineering**, **aerospace**, and **automotive safety** (such as calculating the **impact force** during a **collision** at a specific **deceleration**).
 
• **Relationship:** If the **mass** is doubled while keeping the **acceleration** constant, the **force** required will **double**. Conversely, if **mass** is constant and **acceleration** is doubled, the **force** also **doubles**, showing a **linear relationship**.

questions.question: Three resistors of 4 Omega , 8 Omega , and 12 Omega are connected in series across a 12 {V} battery. The current in the circuit is:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**0.5 A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given resistors of **4 Ω, 8 Ω, and 12 Ω** are connected in **series**. In a series connection, the total or equivalent resistance is the sum of the individual resistances.
 
• The formula to calculate the total resistance in a series circuit is:

 **Rₜₒₜₐₗ = R₁ + R₂ + R₃**.

 Substituting the given values:

 **Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 4 Ω + 8 Ω + 12 Ω = 24 Ω**.
 
• The circuit is powered by a **12 V battery**. Using Ohm's Law, which is **V = IR**, we can calculate the current in the circuit. Rearranging the formula:

 **I = V / R**.
 
• Substitute the values for voltage and total resistance:

 **I = 12 V / 24 Ω = 0.5 A**.
 
• Thus, the current in the circuit is **0.5 A**, which matches the given correct option.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ohm's Law:**

 
 
• **Ohm's Law** states that the current (I) through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage (V) across the two points and inversely proportional to the resistance (R) of the conductor.
 
• The formula is expressed as: **V = IR**, where V is voltage, I is current, and R is resistance.
 
• This law is fundamental in understanding the behavior of electrical circuits.
 
 
 
• **Series Circuit:**
 
 
• In a series circuit, the current remains the same across all components, but the voltage is divided among them.
 
• The total resistance in a series circuit is the sum of all individual resistances: **Rₜₒₜₐₗ = R₁ + R₂ + ... + Rₙ**.
 
 
 
• **Resistors in Series vs. Parallel:**
 
 
• In a series connection, resistors add up to increase the total resistance, while in a parallel connection, the total resistance decreases.
 
• The formula for total resistance in a parallel circuit is:

 **1/Rₜₒₜₐₗ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ... + 1/Rₙ**.
 
 
 
• **Electric Current:**
 
 
• Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor.
 
• The unit of electric current is the **ampere (A)**, named after French physicist André-Marie Ampère.
 
• 1 ampere is equivalent to 1 coulomb of charge passing through a point in 1 second.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Power in an Electrical Circuit:**

 
 
• The power (P) dissipated in an electrical circuit is calculated using the formula: **P = VI**, where V is voltage and I is current.
 
• For resistors, power can also be expressed as: **P = I²R** or **P = V²/R**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Series Circuits:**
 
 
• Series circuits are commonly used in applications where the same current is required to flow through multiple components, such as decorative lights.
 
• However, if one component in the series circuit fails, the entire circuit is interrupted.
 
 
 
• **Units of Measurement:**
 
 
• **Voltage:** Measured in volts (V).
 
• **Resistance:** Measured in ohms (Ω).
 
• **Current:** Measured in amperes (A).

questions.question: A car with a mass of 150 kg is moving at a speed of 36 km/hr. What is the amount of work required to increase its speed to 72 km/hr?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**22,500 J**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The work required to increase the speed of the car can be calculated using the **work-energy theorem**, which states that the work done on an object is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.
 
• The formula for kinetic energy is given as: **K.E. = (1/2)mv²**, where **m** is the mass of the object and **v** is its velocity.
 
• The initial speed of the car is **36 km/hr**, which needs to be converted into meters per second: **36 km/hr = 36 × (1000 / 3600) = 10 m/s**.
 
• The final speed of the car is **72 km/hr**, which is converted into meters per second: **72 km/hr = 72 × (1000 / 3600) = 20 m/s**.
 
• Using the kinetic energy formula, calculate the initial kinetic energy: **K.E. initial = (1/2) × 150 × (10)² = 7500 J**.
 
• Calculate the final kinetic energy: **K.E. final = (1/2) × 150 × (20)² = 30,000 J**.
 
• The work done (or energy required) to increase the speed is the difference in kinetic energies: **Work = K.E. final - K.E. initial = 30,000 J - 7500 J = 22,500 J**.
 
• Therefore, the correct amount of work required is **22,500 J**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kinetic Energy:**

 
 
• Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its motion.
 
• The formula for kinetic energy is: **K.E. = (1/2)mv²**, where **m** is the mass and **v** is the velocity.
 
• It is measured in **joules (J)**, the SI unit of energy.
 
 
 
• **Work-Energy Theorem:**
 
 
• The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.
 
• This principle is crucial for solving problems involving the relationship between work and energy.
 
 
 
• **Conversion of Units:**
 
 
• Speed is often given in **km/hr**, but for physics calculations, it must be converted to **m/s**.
 
• The conversion factor is: **1 km/hr = (1000 / 3600) m/s**.
 
 
 
• **Practical Applications:**
 
 
• Understanding work and energy principles is essential for engineering tasks such as calculating the energy required to accelerate vehicles.
 
• This concept is also used in designing engines, braking systems, and safety measures in automobiles.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Work:**

 
 
• Work is the transfer of energy that occurs when a force is applied over a distance.
 
• Formula: **Work = Force × Distance × cos(θ)**, where **θ** is the angle between the force and displacement direction.
 
 
 
• **Energy Conservation:**
 
 
• The principle of energy conservation states that energy cannot be created or destroyed but can only be transformed from one form to another.
 
• In this case, mechanical energy (kinetic energy) is increased by doing work on the car.
 
 
 
• **SI Units:**
 
 
• Energy is measured in **joules (J)**, and 1 joule is equivalent to 1 newton-meter (N·m).
 
• Speed is measured in **meters per second (m/s)**, and mass is measured in **kilograms (kg)**.
